analysis.one_liner: Strips health insurers' broad antitrust exemption, allowing prosecution of price-fixing and collusion.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Health insurers have long enjoyed a partial antitrust exemption under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, which generally leaves insurance regulation to the states and has been read to shield the 'business of insurance' from federal antitrust laws. This bill would amend that law to say federal antitrust rules fully apply to health insurance, including FTC prohibitions on unfair methods of competition even for nonprofit insurers. In practice, it would expose health insurers to lawsuits and prosecution for collusion, price-fixing, or market allocation. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy health insurance, including people with employer plans and individual market coverage. With antitrust laws fully applying, insurers colluding on prices or dividing markets could be sued, and enforcement could pressure premiums downward in concentrated markets.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the McCarran-Ferguson shield for health insurance, so federal antitrust laws apply to the business of health insurance.
It extends FTC section 5 prohibitions on unfair methods of competition to health insurance whether or not the insurer is organized for profit.
The stated purpose is to protect competition and consumers by restoring antitrust application to health sector insurers.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance companies, which would lose their exemption and face antitrust liability, private treble-damage suits, and FTC oversight. Costs of compliance or settlements could be passed to policyholders in the short run, but the bill's premise is that competition would hold premiums down.

drawbacks.text: Removing the exemption could expose insurers to costly litigation and settlements, and some of those costs could be passed on to policyholders as higher premiums, at least initially.
The bill was narrow: it applied only to health insurance, leaving the McCarran-Ferguson exemption intact for other lines like property and casualty insurance.
Because the bill applied antitrust to health insurers whether or not they operate for profit, even nonprofit insurers would face FTC unfair-competition enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a specific carve-out that shields a highly concentrated industry from competition law. The main downside is potential pass-through of litigation costs to premiums, but the bill's core effect — making colluding health insurers sueable — is one that generally works in consumers' favor. Its narrowness (health insurance only) limited disruption to the broader insurance market.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced May 23, 2011 by Rep. Peter DeFazio with 4 Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on May 23, 2011.
On July 11, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property, Competition and the Internet.
No further action was taken, and the bill died at the end of the 112th Congress without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for another Congress. Consumers gained nothing; the concentrated industry retained its litigation shield.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept their antitrust exemption

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore antitrust laws to health insurance.

for.name: Reps. Louise Slaughter and Gene Green

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat from May 2011 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Benefited from maintaining the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption; historically opposed repeal efforts.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 4 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on. The bill died in committee without a recorded vote, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would end their antitrust exemption, exposing price-fixing and collusion to federal enforcement and private suits. Insurers' interest in keeping the exemption ran against consumers in concentrated markets.
